subtitle: Explain what an agency affirmative action plan is and is not under Minnesota law, tell a workforce goal from a quota, keep goals working on recruitment and process rather than on individual hires, and act on your unit's numbers with their limits in view.
audience: For DHS and DSD supervisors, hiring managers, panel members and program leaders who recruit, select or report on staff, and who want to work confidently with the agency's affirmative action plan and the people who administer it.

lessons.title: What an agency affirmative action plan is, and what it is not
objectives: Describe the statutory basis for affirmative action in Minnesota state employment and the protected groups the statute names.
Identify what an agency plan contains under Minnesota Rules part 3905.0400 and who is accountable for it.
Distinguish what a plan does from what it does not do, including hiring lists, quotas and individual files.
Locate the current agency plan and the person responsible for questions about it.
lessons.teaching:
Affirmative action in Minnesota state employment is set by statute and rule, and a leader who reads those sources will speak more precisely than one who relies on the phrase alone. Minnesota Statutes section 43A.19 directs the commissioner of management and budget to adopt a statewide affirmative action program so that executive branch civil service positions are equally accessible to all qualified persons, and to address past and present discrimination based on protected group status. Section 43A.02, subdivision 33, defines protected groups for affirmative action purposes as females, persons with disabilities, and members of these minorities: Black, Hispanic, Asian or Pacific Islander, and American Indian or Alaskan native. Those are the statute's own terms, and they are narrower than the list of characteristics protected from discrimination.

Each agency head must prepare and carry out an agency affirmative action plan under section 43A.191, and the plan may not be implemented without the commissioner's approval. Agencies with 1,000 or more employees must have at least one full-time affirmative action officer who reports directly to the agency head. Minnesota Rules part 3905.0400 lists what a plan for an agency of 25 or more employees contains: the protected groups that are underrepresented, who is responsible for what, the agency head's commitment, how the program is communicated, a complaint procedure, goals and timetables, programs designed to meet the goals, and how the program is audited and evaluated, including a preemployment review of hiring decisions in goal units with unmet goals. Part 3905.0300 makes the agency head accountable to the governor and the commissioner. Section 43A.19 requires approved plans to be posted on the agency's public and internal websites within 30 days of approval, so you can read your agency's plan rather than guess at it.

It helps just as much to be clear about what a plan is not. It is not a list of people to hire or a quota a manager must fill. It does not lower the qualifications for a job or remove the requirement that selection rest on job-related criteria. It is not a file about individuals; it works with summary data, and section 43A.191 states that no one is required to disclose protected group status. It is not itself a complaint process, though it must include one, and it does not replace the duty to report discrimination or harassment through established channels.

A plan is best read as an accountability document for the agency's processes: where its workforce differs from the qualified labor available, which steps the agency commits to and how it will check whether they worked. That framing matters for advanced practice, because the hard questions are rarely about whether a plan exists. They are about how a goal should influence recruitment, how a review step fits with a hiring manager's judgment and what a leader may and may not say. Questions about the plan's content, its goals or a specific hire go to the agency's affirmative action officer and Human Resources. Formal employment and civil-rights decisions stay with them and with the Equal Opportunity and Access Division; this course prepares you to work with them well.
lessons.keyPoint: An agency affirmative action plan is a public, approved accountability document about the agency's processes. It is not a hiring list, a quota or a file about individuals, and questions about it go to the affirmative action officer and Human Resources.
lessons.example: Practice case: {{NEW_COLLEAGUE}} tells {{CASE_MANAGER}} that a friend in another agency said state managers "have to hire from the affirmative action list" when a job category is short of certain groups. {{NEW_COLLEAGUE}} is about to sit on a hiring panel for the first time and is worried about doing it wrong.
lessons.question: What is the most useful thing for {{CASE_MANAGER}} to say?
choices: Confirm that panels must favor candidates from groups named in the plan when a goal is unmet in that job category.
Explain that the plan sets process goals, not a list of people, and suggest asking the affirmative action officer.
Say affirmative action no longer applies to state agencies because of recent federal changes, so the panel can ignore it.
feedback: This describes a preference in individual selection, which Minnesota's plan does not establish and federal law prohibits. It would give a new panel member a mistaken and risky instruction.
This corrects the misunderstanding without overstating anything. It names what a plan does and points the colleague to the person who can explain how the agency's plan and reviews actually work.
Minnesota's statutes and rules on agency plans remain in place, and federal guidance has not removed them. Telling a panel to ignore the plan replaces one mistake with another.
lessons.reflection: Privately consider what you believed about affirmative action in state hiring before this lesson, and where that belief came from. Which part, if any, would you now want to check against the agency's actual plan?
lessons.action: Find your agency's current approved affirmative action plan on its public or internal website. Note who the affirmative action officer is, which sections cover goals and hiring review, and one question you would like to ask about how the plan applies to your area.

check.question: Which statement accurately describes an agency affirmative action plan under Minnesota law?
check.correct: It is prepared by the agency head, approved by the commissioner and posted publicly, and it sets goals for agency processes.
wrong: It is a confidential list of candidates from protected groups that hiring managers must consider first.
It replaces the agency's complaint process for concerns about discrimination and harassment in hiring.
check.feedback: Section 43A.191 requires the agency head to prepare the plan and the commissioner to approve it, and section 43A.19 requires approved plans to be posted. A plan includes a complaint procedure but does not replace the duty to report through established channels, and it is not a candidate list.

lessons.title: Goals versus quotas: how a goal is set and what it may not do
objectives: Explain how goals are set for goal units under Minnesota Rules part 3905.0600 and section 43A.19.
Distinguish a workforce goal from a quota and from a preference in an individual decision.
Summarize what Title VII and current EEOC technical assistance say about protected characteristics in employment actions.
Name the tension between the state rule on considering goals and federal law, and route it to the people who interpret it.
lessons.teaching:
Minnesota's goals come from a defined method, not from a manager's sense of balance. Section 43A.19 directs the commissioner to set statewide goals for each federal Equal Employment Opportunity occupational category, considering at least the share of each protected class in the recruiting area's population with the necessary skills and the availability of current employees for promotion or transfer. Under Minnesota Rules part 3905.0600, agencies use labor force data, apply statistical formulas to identify underutilization, set a goal for a protected group in a goal unit when that unit underutilizes the group, and base timetables on turnover and hire rates in each goal unit. A goal unit, as section 43A.02 defines it, is the group of jobs in an agency or agency subdivision assigned to one EEO occupational category. It is usually not the same thing as your team.

A goal describes a gap between the workforce and the qualified labor available, and it asks the agency to work on the processes that produce the gap. A quota would require a set number of people from a group to be selected regardless of the candidates. Federal law draws a firm line here. Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which covers state governments as employers, makes it unlawful to refuse to hire or otherwise discriminate against an individual because of race, color, religion, sex or national origin. Section 703(j) states that Title VII does not require preferential treatment because of an imbalance in the workforce, and section 703(l) prohibits adjusting scores, using different cutoff scores or otherwise altering employment test results on the basis of those characteristics.

Federal enforcement positions have also tightened. The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission's technical assistance on discrimination connected to workplace diversity initiatives, issued in 2025 and described as non-binding, says an employment action motivated in whole or in part by race, sex or another protected characteristic can be unlawful, and that Title VII contains no "diversity interest" exception. In February 2026 the commission's chair sent a letter to large employers repeating those points. These documents interpret the law rather than rewrite it, and they do not address every state practice. They do make clear that a protected characteristic cannot be a factor in choosing a particular person.

That creates a tension an advanced leader should name rather than smooth over. Minnesota Rules part 3905.0100 says good-faith effort requires, at a minimum, consideration of affirmative action goals on all staffing and personnel decisions. Many leaders keep the two consistent by letting the goal shape the process, such as where a job is advertised, how criteria are written and whether a review takes place, while keeping the choice of a person on job-related evidence. Whether that is the complete answer, and how the rule is applied today, is a question for the affirmative action officer, Human Resources and legal counsel, and the answer may shift as federal guidance and court decisions change. Do not settle it yourself, and do not tell a panel what a goal means for a particular hire.
lessons.keyPoint: A goal measures a gap between a goal unit's workforce and the qualified labor available and directs effort at processes. It never authorizes using a protected characteristic in choosing a person, and questions about where that line falls go to the affirmative action officer, Human Resources and legal counsel.
lessons.example: Practice case: At a supervisors' meeting, {{SUPERVISOR}} shares that a job category in the division has an unmet goal. Another supervisor suggests that when two finalists are close, panels could "use the goal as the tiebreaker." Several people nod, and {{PROGRAM_MANAGER}} is asked for a view.
lessons.question: How should {{PROGRAM_MANAGER}} respond?
choices: Say a tiebreaker uses a protected characteristic to choose a person, and suggest asking HR how goals can shape process.
Support the tiebreaker, since it only applies when candidates are already equally qualified and the rule says to consider goals.
Suggest using the tiebreaker informally without recording it, so the decision cannot be challenged later.
feedback: This names the problem directly and keeps the goal in play where it belongs. Asking Human Resources and the affirmative action officer how goals can shape outreach, criteria and review puts the interpretation with the people responsible for it.

This is a believable reading of the state rule, but it applies the goal to the choice of a person. Federal law and current EEOC guidance treat an action motivated in part by a protected characteristic as potentially unlawful, so this needs expert review, not a meeting consensus.
Keeping a practice off the record does not make it lawful, and it undermines the documentation that selection reviews depend on. It also exposes candidates and the agency to harm.
lessons.reflection: Privately think about the difference between wanting a more representative workforce and wanting a particular hire to turn out a certain way. Where in your own work could the first slide into the second without anyone noticing?
lessons.action: Write down one way a workforce goal could shape a process you are involved in, such as where a posting is shared or how a criterion is worded. Then write one way it must not shape a decision. Ask the affirmative action officer whether your examples match current agency guidance.

check.question: What distinguishes a workforce goal from a quota?
check.correct: A goal identifies a gap and directs effort at processes; a quota requires selecting a set number of people from a group.
wrong: A goal applies only to promotions, while a quota applies only to new hires from outside.
A goal is set by the agency itself, while a quota is set by the federal government for it.
check.feedback: Goals under Minnesota Rules part 3905.0600 compare a goal unit's workforce with available qualified labor and set targets and timetables for agency effort. A quota would dictate selections by group, which Title VII does not permit. Neither term depends on the type of personnel action or which government sets it.

lessons.title: How goals inform recruitment and selection without deciding a hire
objectives: Identify where MMB Policy 1434 connects affirmative action goals to recruitment and selection.
Examine criteria and tools for requirements that narrow the pool without reflecting the work.
Explain the purpose of pre-hire review and justification steps and how a leader should respond to them.
Practice language that keeps protected status out of statements about individual hires.
lessons.teaching:
If a goal shapes the process rather than the person, the leader's work is in the process. MMB's Recruitment and Selection Policy, HR/LR Policy 1434, most recently revised in October 2025, says a longer public posting period supports state affirmative action goals, requires agencies to follow all affirmative action and equal opportunity requirements and says announcements should go to targeted and diverse recruitment sources. Broad outreach does not decide who is hired. It changes who learns about a job and applies, which is where many gaps begin.

Criteria and tools come next. The policy says screening criteria must be job-related, and that screening and selection materials such as interview questions, scoring matrices and assessments should be approved by the agency HR office or affirmative action officer. That review is a chance to ask whether a requirement describes the work or a familiar background. A preferred qualification that few qualified people could hold unless they followed one path, an exercise timed in a way the job is not, or a question that rewards a particular style can narrow the pool before anyone is compared. The policy also says initial communications should invite applicants with disabilities to request reasonable accommodation, which keeps access from depending on whether a candidate knows to ask.

Review steps sit at the end. The policy uses a Pre-Hire Justification Form to show that the finalist selected for an offer is the top-ranked candidate using job-related criteria, and the hiring supervisor cannot make an offer until the form is reviewed and signed. Minnesota Rules part 3905.0400 calls for a preemployment review of hiring decisions in goal units with unmet goals, and section 43A.191 expects an agency that misses its hiring goals to justify its nonaffirmative action hires under criteria the department issues, alongside active recruitment, a retention plan and a complaint procedure. A leader should understand these reviews as a check on whether the process was fair and documented. They are not a second vote on the candidate, and they are not an obstacle to route around.

A few habits keep the line clear. Record the evidence for your ranking in job-related terms before anyone discusses workforce figures. Do not ask a panel to weigh a goal when rating candidates, and do not tell a candidate or a colleague that someone was hired, or not hired, because of a group. If a reviewer asks a question, answer it with the record rather than with reassurance about the person. If you believe the criteria themselves screened out qualified people, raise that for the next posting instead of changing the standard partway through this one. When you are unsure what a review requires, ask the affirmative action officer before the offer, not after it.
lessons.keyPoint: Goals do their work before and around a selection: in outreach, in job-related criteria and in review of whether the process was fair. The choice of a person rests on job-related evidence, documented before anyone discusses workforce figures.
lessons.example: Practice case: {{SUPERVISOR}} has selected a finalist and submits the pre-hire paperwork. The affirmative action officer asks why the posting required a specific degree when the class specification lists equivalent experience, and why the interview included a timed writing exercise. {{SUPERVISOR}} is frustrated, because the finalist is clearly strong.
lessons.question: What is the best way for {{SUPERVISOR}} to respond?
choices: Explain that the finalist is the strongest candidate and ask the officer to approve the offer so the team is not left short.
Withdraw the finalist and reopen the posting, since any question from the officer means the process has failed.
Answer from the record, explain how each criterion relates to the job, and ask what to change for the next posting.
feedback: The officer's question is about the process, not the candidate. Reassurance about the person does not answer it and treats the review as a hurdle rather than a check.
A question is not a finding. Reopening without understanding the concern wastes effort, may be unnecessary and does not improve the criteria for next time.
This treats the review as intended. It answers with documented, job-related reasons and opens the door to improving criteria for future postings without changing the standard for this one.
lessons.reflection: Privately recall a requirement in a posting you have written or used, or use the degree requirement in the practice case. What would you say if someone asked how it relates to the work? Is that answer written down anywhere?
lessons.action: Before your next posting or panel, list each minimum and preferred qualification and each selection exercise. Beside each, write one sentence on how it relates to the work. Share the list with Human Resources or the affirmative action officer and ask whether anything should change.

check.question: Under MMB Policy 1434, what does the Pre-Hire Justification Form show?
check.correct: That the finalist selected for an offer is the top-ranked candidate using job-related criteria.
wrong: That the finalist belongs to a protected group named in the agency plan.
That the hiring supervisor has consulted the finalist's references and former supervisors.
check.feedback: The policy uses the form to document that the selected finalist ranks highest on job-related criteria, and no offer may be made until it is reviewed and signed. It does not record group membership and is not a reference check.

lessons.title: Reading your unit's numbers and acting on them
objectives: Ask the questions that clarify what a workforce figure counts, covers and compares against.
Explain how self-reporting, small numbers and goal-unit boundaries limit what unit data can show.
Trace a pattern along the employment path from applicant to separation to find processes a leader can influence.
Plan a process change with an owner, a review date and honest limits on what later figures can show.
lessons.teaching:
Workforce numbers reach leaders in several forms: the agency plan, MMB's statewide progress report, internal dashboards or a summary from the affirmative action officer. Section 43A.191 requires the commissioner to report each agency's and the state's progress to the Governor and legislative committees by March 1 of each odd-numbered year and to post the report publicly, and to publish annual summary data on protected group hiring by federal EEO occupational category. Before acting on any figure, ask what it counts, which goal unit and period it covers, whether it describes the current workforce, hires or separations, and what group of jobs and labor market it compares against.

Numbers about protected groups have limits that a leader should respect. Membership is self-reported, and no one is required to disclose it, so counts can understate some groups and can shift when people update their records. Small numbers move sharply: in a unit of twelve, one hire or one departure can swing a percentage widely and can point to individuals. A goal set for an agency goal unit may not translate into anything meaningful for a single team. Treat a unit figure as a prompt for questions about process, not as a verdict about anyone, and ask the affirmative action officer how data may be shared before you discuss it with others.

Useful questions follow the path a person takes through employment. Where do applicants come from, and do qualified people from protected groups apply but drop out at screening, interview or offer? Are the minimum and preferred qualifications narrower than the work requires? Who leaves, after how long, and what do stay and exit conversations suggest? Section 43A.19 asks for analysis of separation patterns and their effect on protected group members, because retention can undo recruitment. Who receives the development and acting roles that lead to the next job? These questions point to things a leader can influence: outreach, proposals for criteria, panel preparation, onboarding, accommodation follow-through and fair access to opportunity.

Acting well means changing processes and documenting reasons, not adjusting a particular decision to move a number. Bring the pattern and a proposed change to Human Resources and the affirmative action officer, agree on who owns the change and set a time to look again. Be honest about what a later figure can show; a change may reflect a hiring wave, a reorganization or better data rather than your step. A leader answers for the fairness and transparency of the processes in their area, for completing required reviews, for routing concerns promptly and for keeping protected status out of individual decisions. When a question concerns the plan, its goals or a specific hire, take it to the affirmative action officer and Human Resources, and expect the answer to come from them.
lessons.keyPoint: Unit numbers are prompts for questions about process, not verdicts about people. Leaders act by changing outreach, criteria, onboarding and access to opportunity with Human Resources and the affirmative action officer, never by adjusting an individual decision.
lessons.example: Practice case: A summary from the affirmative action officer shows that a DSD goal unit has had an unmet goal for three years. {{PROGRAM_MANAGER}} also learns from the summary that qualified applicants from the underutilized group applied in numbers close to labor availability but were less often invited to interview. {{PROGRAM_MANAGER}} wants to respond before the next round of postings.
lessons.question: What should {{PROGRAM_MANAGER}} do first?
choices: Ask HR and the affirmative action officer to review screening criteria and resume scoring, and set a review date.
Tell supervisors to interview every applicant from the underutilized group, so the interview numbers come into line.
Wait for another year of data, since three years of figures for one goal unit may simply reflect chance.
feedback: The data points to a specific stage, screening, and this response examines it with the people responsible. It changes the process for everyone and builds in a check on whether the change helped.
Guaranteeing interviews by group uses a protected characteristic in an individual step of selection. It may change a number while creating a serious legal and fairness problem.
Caution about small numbers is reasonable, but this pattern is specific and has persisted. Reviewing screening criteria is low-risk and can proceed while the data continues to be watched.
lessons.reflection: Privately consider how you usually react to a workforce figure that looks worse than you expected. Do you tend to look for a person to explain it, a process to examine, or a reason to set it aside?
lessons.action: Ask the affirmative action officer what summary workforce information is available for the goal units your area hires into, and how it may be shared. Choose one stage of the employment path to examine, name an owner for any change and set a date to review it.

check.question: Why can a single team's percentage be misleading as a measure of progress on an affirmative action goal?
check.correct: Goals are set for goal units that may be larger than a team, and small counts can swing widely and point to individuals.
wrong: Teams are not allowed to see any workforce data about their own members under Minnesota law.
Percentages are calculated only for agencies with more than 1,000 employees in a goal unit.
check.feedback: A goal unit is a group of jobs in an agency or subdivision assigned to one EEO category, not a team. With small counts, one hire or departure changes a percentage sharply and may identify someone. Summary data is published, and agency size does not determine whether percentages are calculated.

cards.back: Under Minnesota Statutes section 43A.02, subdivision 33: females, persons with disabilities, and members of these minorities: Black, Hispanic, Asian or Pacific Islander, and American Indian or Alaskan native.
Prepared by the agency head under section 43A.191, approved by the commissioner and posted publicly. It sets goals and steps for agency processes, not a list of people.
The group of jobs in an agency or agency subdivision assigned to one federal EEO occupational category. Goals are set by goal unit, which is usually not the same as a team.

A goal identifies a gap between a goal unit's workforce and available qualified labor and directs effort at processes. A quota would require selecting a set number of people by group; Title VII does not permit that.
Title VII does not require preferential treatment because of a workforce imbalance, and it prohibits adjusting scores or cutoffs on the basis of race, color, religion, sex or national origin.

Minnesota Rules part 3905.0100 calls for result-oriented procedures and consideration of goals on staffing decisions. How that applies to an individual hire today is a question for the affirmative action officer, HR and legal counsel.

MMB Policy 1434 requires a reviewed and signed Pre-Hire Justification Form showing the finalist is top-ranked on job-related criteria before any offer. It checks the process, not the candidate's group.

aid.heading: Know the plan
items: Read your agency's current approved plan and note the affirmative action officer's name.
Identify which goal units your area hires into and whether any have unmet goals.
Remember that the plan sets goals for processes and is not a list of people or a quota.
Take plan questions to the affirmative action officer and Human Resources.

aid.heading: Let goals shape the process
items: Share postings through broad and targeted recruitment sources and allow time for people to apply.
Write a job-related reason beside every qualification and selection exercise.
Invite accommodation requests in initial communications with applicants.
Have selection materials reviewed by HR or the affirmative action officer before use.

aid.heading: Keep protected status out of individual decisions
items: Record ranking evidence in job-related terms before anyone discusses workforce figures.
Never ask a panel to weigh a goal or use one as a tiebreaker.
Answer review questions from the record, and ask before the offer if unsure.
Never tell anyone a person was hired or not hired because of a group.

aid.heading: Read and act on numbers
items: Ask what a figure counts, which goal unit and period it covers and what it compares against.
Treat small counts with caution and protect individuals when sharing data.
Trace patterns from applicant to separation and pick one stage to examine.
Name an owner and a review date for each change, and be honest about what later figures can show.

sources.title: Minnesota Statutes section 43A.19 (affirmative action)
sources.note: Supports the statewide program's purpose, goals by EEO occupational category and the factors used, analysis of separation patterns and posting of approved agency plans within 30 days (lessons 1, 2 and 4). Amended as recently as 2025; check the current text.

sources.title: Minnesota Statutes section 43A.02 (definitions)
sources.note: Subdivision 33 defines protected groups for affirmative action purposes and subdivision 22c defines a goal unit (lessons 1 and 2). The definitions use the statute's own terms.

sources.title: Minnesota Statutes section 43A.191 (agency affirmative action programs)
sources.note: Supports the agency head's duty to prepare a plan, commissioner approval, affirmative action officers, justification of nonaffirmative action hires when goals are unmet, biennial progress reporting, summary data and the statement that no one must disclose protected group status (lessons 1, 3 and 4).

sources.title: Minnesota Rules chapter 3905 (affirmative action)
sources.note: Parts 3905.0100, 0300, 0400 and 0600 support good-faith effort, agency head accountability, plan contents including preemployment review, and how underutilization, goals and timetables are set (lessons 1 to 3). Published 2009; read with current statutes and federal law.

sources.title: MMB HR/LR Policy 1434: Recruitment and Selection
sources.note: Supports the links between posting periods, recruitment sources and affirmative action goals, job-related screening criteria, review of selection materials and the Pre-Hire Justification Form (lesson 3). Revised October 20, 2025; confirm agency procedure with HR.

sources.title: EEOC — Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964
sources.note: Supports the prohibition on discrimination in hiring, sections 703(j) and 703(l), and coverage of governmental employers (lesson 2). Application to a particular practice is a question for legal counsel.

sources.title: EEOC — What You Should Know About DEI-Related Discrimination at Work
sources.note: Supports the statements that an action motivated in whole or in part by a protected characteristic may be unlawful and that Title VII has no diversity-interest exception (lesson 2). Non-binding technical assistance from 2025; the related February 2026 letter from the EEOC chair repeats these points. Check for later changes.
